Place the index, middle and ring fingers of one hand in front of the ear, from top to bottom: TE21, SI19 and GB2, in the hollows you feel when you open your mouth. Press slowly with medium, comfortable pressure (4–6/10) forward, keeping your mouth slightly open, then repeat on the other side.

Place your thumbs at the nose end of the eyebrow, in the notch of the bone (BL2), on the bone, not behind it, and press gently upward, toward the forehead, without pushing toward the eye. With the tips of your index fingers, at the same time, press on the brow bone, level with EX-HN4, at the middle of the eyebrow. Never press on the eyeball.

Place a tennis ball between your back and the wall, to the side of the spine, and make small knee bends to roll it over the muscle. Stay 20–30 s on tender spots, without sharp pain. The ball must not touch the spine or bone directly.

Place the heel of your palm or the fleshy part of your forearm on the muscle and let your body weight provide the pressure, not the strength of your arm. Slide slowly or stay still for 10–20 s. Keep asking your partner how it feels.

Place the pad of your thumb on the point and increase the pressure gradually, over 3–5 seconds, until you feel a firm but bearable pressure. Hold steady while breathing slowly, then release slowly. Do not repeat more than 2–3 times on the same point in one session.

Place the tips of your index fingers in the grooves next to the wings of the nose, on both LI20, and press gently toward the bone, upward and inward, for 20–30 seconds, then gently in small circles. Then, separately, press with your middle finger between the eyebrows (Yintang) for 15–20 seconds.

With the middle finger of one hand, press rhythmically on GV20, at the crown of the head, and with the middle finger of the other hand press on Taiyang, on one side, with presses of 2–3 seconds. Breathe deeply and alertly for 30–45 seconds, then switch temples.

With two fingers of one hand, apply light pressure on CV12, at the midpoint of the line between the lower sternum and the navel. At the same time, with one finger of the other hand, press gently on ST25, 2 finger-widths lateral to the navel. Breathe slowly into your belly for 45–60 seconds, then on the other side.
With a fever or poor general condition, postpone the massage until you have recovered.
With lymphedema or after removal of lymph nodes, do not massage the limb without your doctor's approval.

With the opposite hand, grasp the forearm: thumb on LI10, 2 cun below the elbow crease, on the muscle, and the tip of the middle finger on LI11, at the outer end of the crease of the bent elbow. Press both at once, gently and deeply, then slightly extend and bend the arm.

With the opposite hand, grasp the shoulder: tip of the index finger in the hollow in front of the acromion (LI15), and tip of the thumb in the hollow behind it (TE14), like a pincer. Press both at once, gently and deeply, then make small slow movements of the arm if you feel comfortable.

With the opposite hand, grasp the wrist: thumb on PC6, between the two tendons, 2 finger-widths above the wrist crease, and the tip of the index or middle finger on HT7, in the crease, on the little-finger side. Press both at once, light to medium (3–5/10), for 60 seconds, with slow breaths; stop at tingling, numbness or a shock-like sensation in the fingers; switch hands.

With the opposite hand, place your thumb on LI4, in the muscle between the thumb and index finger, and the tip of your index finger on SI3, on the ulnar edge of the hand, behind the joint of the little finger, when the fist is slightly clenched. If you cannot reach both points at once, press them in turn, 20–30 seconds each, with comfortable medium pressure, then switch hands.

With the opposite hand, place your thumb on PC6 on the palm side and your index finger on TE5, exactly opposite, on the back of the forearm. Squeeze gently, like a pincer, keeping the pressure constant and breathing slowly.

With a relaxed hand, tap quickly and lightly with the edge of the hand (the little-finger side) or with a cupped hand, alternating hands. The movement comes from the wrist, not the shoulder, and the taps are springy, not heavy. If a tap feels “in the bone,” stop and move your hand to a thicker muscle.

With one hand, place your thumb on KI3, in the hollow between the inner ankle bone and the Achilles tendon, and your index finger on BL60, exactly opposite, between the outer ankle bone and the tendon. Squeeze gently like a pincer for 60 seconds, then switch feet.

With one hand, place your thumb on LR3, on the top of the foot, in the hollow where the metatarsal bones of toes 1 and 2 meet. With the other hand, press with your thumb on SP4, in the arch of the foot, on the inner edge. Press both at once, with medium, comfortable pressure (4–6/10), for 60 seconds.
